Patient Vignette: "Mara" (Age 27, Non-binary, Oceania)

Mara arrives to sessions with a quiet, deliberate stillness, as though they are constantly listening for something just out of earshot. They are a special education teacher at a public elementary school, a role they describe with a mix of fierce protectiveness and bone-deep exhaustion. Their partner, Alex, often waits for them in the car after sessions, a quiet anchor in the parking lot.

The story Mara tells begins about fourteen months ago, when they were 26. They had just started a new relationship with Alex, and were feeling hopeful for the first time in years. That same month, a parent of one of their students-a man named Mr. Vance-began waiting for Mara after school. At first, it seemed like concern. He wanted to talk about his son's IEP, about sensory breaks, about Mara's "methods." But the conversations grew longer, and his questions turned personal. He began appearing at the coffee shop Mara visited every morning, then at the grocery store on their weekly shopping night. He knew their schedule. He knew their car. He left a note under their windshield wiper one cold November morning: "You understand him. No one else does. You're special."

Mara's heart first cracked open on a Tuesday in December. They were in the classroom after hours, laminating visual schedules, when they heard the tap of a key in the lock. The door swung open. Mr. Vance stood there, holding a thermos of tea. "I thought you might be cold," he said. He had a master key. He had a copy of the building's after-hours access code. Mara froze. They thanked him, took the tea, and did not drink it. They did not report it. They told themselves he was just a lonely, over-involved parent. They told Alex it was "nothing."

Over the next six weeks, the stalking escalated. He called the school's main line, pretending to be a district supervisor, asking for Mara's personal cell number. He stood outside their apartment building on a Saturday morning, just watching the windows. Mara began taking different routes to work, leaving at unpredictable times, checking the back seat of their car before getting in. They stopped going to the grocery store. They stopped going to the café. They stopped leaving the apartment after dark.

The breaking point came in late January. Mara was leaving a staff meeting at 5:30 PM, and Mr. Vance was leaning against their car, arms crossed, smiling. "I just wanted to say goodnight," he said. "You work too hard." Mara's legs went numb. They walked back into the school, called Alex, and then called the police. A restraining order was filed. Mr. Vance was arrested for trespassing and later charged with stalking. He was banned from school property. He is currently awaiting trial.

Now, ten months later, Mara still teaches. But the classroom is no longer a sanctuary. They flinch when a parent knocks on the door. They scan every face at pickup, cataloging features-height, hair color, the shape of a jaw. They have installed a deadbolt on their apartment door, and they check it three times before sleeping. Alex sleeps on the side closest to the door, and Mara has asked them to keep a baseball bat under the bed. Mara has not returned to the coffee shop. They have not gone to the grocery store alone in eight months.

Mara's sleep is fractured. They wake at 3:17 AM most nights-the time Mr. Vance left the note-with their heart hammering, convinced they heard a key in the lock. They have nightmares of being trapped in the classroom, of the door opening and opening and never stopping. During the day, they feel hypervigilant: they scan crowds, they avoid eye contact with strangers, they jump at the sound of a car backfiring. They have lost five pounds because they cannot eat in public spaces, and they have stopped eating lunch in the staff lounge because someone might walk up behind them.

At work, Mara is still effective-their students need them, and they refuse to let Mr. Vance take that. But they have stopped staying late. They have stopped decorating the classroom door. They have stopped trusting the kindness of strangers. Their partner, Alex, is patient and steady, but Mara often feels like a ghost in their own life-present, but untouchable. They do not feel safe. They do not know if they will ever feel safe again.
